newsitem.title: GERMANY: Oilseeds industry seen escaping gene-food protests.
newsitem.headline: Oilseeds industry seen escaping gene-food protests.

text.p: Oilseeds industry sources believe renewed campaigns against the sale of genetically modified food in Europe will spare soybean processors and instead focus on food companies and maize growers.
"Processors have not changed their intake of imported soybeans and there is no demand for beans or products free of genetic modifications," a leading German seeds broker said.
"I consider the subject closed."
His remarks came a day after environmental group Greenpeace started a new round of protest at food firms in nine European countries against genetically-modified soybeans and grains.
Activists blockaded offices belonging to Nestle, Unilever and Danone in a campaign targetting soybeans developed by U.S. chemicals firm Monsanto and maize from Swiss company Ciba Geigy AG.
But they failed to obtain assurances the firms would go without genetically modified soy in their products, which Greenpeace says may bear unknown health risks.
Greenpeace also attacked a new European law on "novel foods," which lays down rules for marketing and labelling, saying it has too many loopholes and tells consumers nothing.

An official at the German seed crushers organisation VDO, which represents mills supplying vegetable oils to food firms, said crushing plants had not reported overall lower soy oil sales or higher demand for non-modified soy oil.
"Crushers who nevertheless tried to get non-modified soybeans couldn't secure the volumes they needed at a reasonable cost," she said.
"It could not be completely ruled out that even these shipments were entirely free of modified beans," she said.
American soybean farmers had signalled the share of modified beans in the 1997/98 crop may rise to 10 or 12 percent from less than two percent in this year's crop, she added.
A separation, demanded by Greenpeace, was not planned.
Food firms had dismissed the latest campaign because there were no new arguments, said an official at food industry institute BLL, which provides legal and scientific services.
The industry would fully comply with the "novel food" law.
Greenpeace said on Tuesday it would next try to stop planned cultivation of genetically-altered maize in Europe, which may be offered in time for spring plantings here.
It sees even greater health risks from maize than from soya and points out it will be grown here rather than imported.
An official at German plant breeders association BDP in Bonn said the discussion about the planting of genetically modified maize needed to be scientific and not emotional.
"BDP and farmers are aiming to pre-empt protests and inform the public about the merits of the new crops," she said.
In the markets, soybean importers baulked at high dollar prices which squeezed operating margins and made soymeal less competitive against other meals, including domestic rape meal.
Rapeseed prices were rising on meal demand but also on expanding rape oil sales, where the premium over soy oil, acquired during the anti-soya campaign, was shrinking fast.
This, combined with weaker European currencies, boosted EU rape oil export chances versus Latin America's soy oil offers.
But European rapeseed supply will remain tight due to harvest losses in 1996 and crushers will have to use more sunseed and soybeans in order to utilise their capacity.
